I never referred to the very fine staff of the Department of External Affairs, or to the head of it, the

The house resumed from Thursday, March 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fernand Viau for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.
Mr. ANGUS MaeINNIS (Vancouver East): Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne usually outlines the policy of the government for the session. When I heard the speech read by His Excellency at the opening of parliament my reaction was a hope that the people of Canada were not looking for very much this year, because if they were, and if there is not something more in the government's programme than there is in the speech, they certainly will be disappointed. In the speech last year it was mentioned that we were building a new world. As we did not finish that job last year I thought there might be something in the speech this year to indicate that we might be going on with that job. But there is nothing of the kind in the speech. There is no reference to the brave new world. As a matter of fact the speech gives every indication of being the work of tired men who are looking backward to the old world rather than forward to a new one.
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

I represent a working class constituency. I have a fairly long association with organized labour and other working class movements, so I wish to say something about the aspirations and the fears of the working people, not only of my own constituency but of Canada, as I see and understand them.
Perhaps the greatest fear to-day among the workers is that of unemployment, the fear that we may be slipping back to the days and the conditions prior to 1939-and I have a fairly good idea that other people besides the workers have this same fear.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) replied to the criticism of the leader of tne opposition (Mr. Bracken) last Monday on unemployment, he brushed that criticism aside by asking this question: Though employment is not all that we would wish it to be, where is there a country better off than Canada?
An lion. MEMBER: Hear, hear.
Mr. MaeINNIS: My hon. friend says "hear, hear." Then the Prime Minister went on to compare conditions in Canada with those in the United Kingdom, Belgium, Holland and other parts of Europe. Such sophistry is begging the question, because conditions in Canada are not comparable with conditions in the United Kingdom or in the countries of Europe. The war destroyed the economy of almost the whole of Europe; and in the United Kingdom, if the country's economy was not destroyed by war, the whole economy was converted to war purposes. But in Canada the same war made this country greater and richer and more able to provide for the people than ever it was before. So it is sheer nonsense to compare conditions in Canada at the present time with conditions in almost any other part of the world. Perhaps the only comparable country is the republic to the south'of us. The fact of the matter is that at the present time we have unemployment on a large scale. I would urge the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other members of the cabinet not to be too offhand about it, because the 263,000 who were unemployed at the date of the last report, and the others who do not know how soon they also may be unemployed, are not offhanded about it. Perhaps of itself 263,000 is not an alarming number; but it is alarming in view of the world's need and Canada's need of goods.
I am aware of the fact that unemployment is not yet acute, that there is no mass suffering such as we had in the thirties. The reason of course is that we have made some provision against it. There are the unemployment insurance benefits; there are also the

sayings made during the war when work was plentiful, and service pay, and the like. But these resources, however large they may be, are limited, and are a mere stop-gap. What is causing the workers worry to-day is not so much the present unemployment, although it is bad enough, but the fact that no plan is being prepared to obviate the conditions which brought about such disastrous results in the thirties. There are no plans for public welfare, and the position of the average worker is as- it always has been-the harder he works the sooner he is looking for another job. Until we get away from that, and the worker has assurance of continuity of income, there will always be that worry.
The only reference in the speech from the throne to unemployment is typical of the old thinking in the new world upon which we are entering. I read from Hansard, page 1:
The maintenance of a high level of employment and national income is a fundamental aim of government policy. Employment and income alike are bound up with the restoration -and expansion of world trade. To the productive employment of vast numbers of Canadians, export markets are essential.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is old stuff. It was dinned into our ears all during the depression. I appreciate as much as anyone does the value of export trade, but export trade will not put an end to unemployment and distress in this country; it will make for unemployment unless we are prepared to make trade a two-way affair. That is, unless we are prepared to accept imports in the full measure of our exports and to distribute to our people the national income so created, foreign trade will not help us very much. I believe we shall have to approach full employment, the elimination of unemployment, in a time of peace in somewhat the same way as we proceeded during the war. We put an end to unemployment during the war, not by trying to find work or to make work for people, but by producing the needs of war. Now, with peace here, there are peace-time needs, and if we put our people to work to satisfy the needs of peace, to provide the things which our people need in their everyday life, not only shall we find work for everyone, but there will be more jobs than workers, as there were during the war.
There are other measures to which I wish to refer, but before I do so I want to say that I believe that labour in Canada deserves the appreciation of the government and of the people for the freedom from industrial strife enjoyed by this country since the end of hostilities. The smoothness with which

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
production and services were carried on at a time when wages were falling and prices rising has been of tremendous advantage to this country. In that respect the situation here has been quite different from what it has been on the other side of the border. But organized labour will demand wage increases, and will demand them because they have become necessary. Now that the war is over and there is more civilian production, labour is entitled to a higher, not a lower, standard of living. High wages are also necessary because high wages will help to prevent another depression. In our capitalist economy depressions always come about when there is an over-supply of goods for which there is a need, but those who have the need have not the price to buy. Therefore, higher wages will help to prevent another depression.
During the war there was a ceiling on wages. I agree that it was necessary to stabilize wages, although I have always maintained in this house and outside that to the extent that a stable price structure was maintained, to that extent the burden was borne by the low-paid wage and salary earner. I suggest that the government should not wait for strikes and disputes before there is an increase in wages. The government should make it quite clear that it is in favour of increases in wages at the present time.
There will also be a demand for shorter hours. The two national labour bodies, the trades and labour congress and the Canadian congress of labour, have gone on record in favour of a forty-hour week without reduction in pay. This will mean, if it does come about, that where there is a forty-four hour week and it is reduced to forty, a ten per cent wage increase will be required, and if it is forty-eight hours reduced to forty, the necessary wage increase will be twenty per cent. There are many industries in Canada in which the work week is much higher than forty-eight hours and even fifty-six hours a week.
While we are discussing shorter hours we should not lose sight of the world's tremendous needs for production. I suggest to the Minister of Labour and the government that they should take into consideration the calling of a conference of representatives of organized labour, organized employers and the government to discuss the best means of attaining full production and full employment. Such conferences have taken place in the United Kingdom, and . I believe they have been productive of much good.
I am suggesting such a conference because I believe that full production at this time is exceedingly important. I notice that the Minister of Labour ip a recent speech at Renfrew said:
We must use the same characteristic good sense which we used when our backs were to the wall, and then the Canadian people will be able to overcome any difficulties which we may face.
I agree with the minister that, united, we can overcome any of our difficulties in Canada, and I suppose almost everyone will agree with him in that. But I should be astonished if the minister finds the same attitude towards that sort of cooperation to-day as he found during the war. Indeed, the whole cry for the removal of controls is to get away from working together and back to the old system of everyone for himself and the dievil take the hindmost.
It has been suggested by the two labour congresses.

Yes. That was the motive behind this demand for the removal of controls, and we still hear it. They want a restoration of freedom. I am wondering what freedom -freedom to do the other fellow before he does you? It is because we have no common objective and because we want to get back to the principles of free enterprise that we are told by these lovers of freedom that we must get rid of the bureaucrats. The people who suggest this are unconscious of the fact that the bureaucrats, if there are any, came into being to protect the community from irresponsible private bureaucrats.
Pirates.

"Pirates" is right. The question of the removal of wage control and price control has been receiving considerable attention, particularly the matter of wage control, by organized labour. Personally I cannot at the moment see that any advantage could accrue to labour by the removal of wage control.
I agree with my hon. friend.

I am sure the minister does. As regards labour, the supply to-day is greater than the demand, while other commodities are in the opposite position, the demand being greater than the supply. If we removed all the controls, prices would skyrocket and it would be very difficult to get wage increases at all. I do not see, therefore, that there is any hope in that direction. I believe, however, that labour should be allowed to negotiate for fairly substantial increases, not only because of the increased
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

cost of living but also because of the increased amount of consumers' goods that are coming into the market. For these reasons, the low-paid workers particularly should be allowed to negotiate for substantial increases in wages.
Seyeral hon. members have urged that the income tax exemptions should be raised to $2,000. Of course this matter is not dealt with in the speech from the throne; it falls more naturally under the budget, but it has been mentioned. I am in favour of raising the exemption on the income tax [DOT] to $2,000, but I would much rather see this house take some action to ensure that every family received an income of $2,000. It is not of much use to have the exemption raised on an income one does not receive.
I shall give the house some examples of workers' wages in Canada in 1941 when the wages were frozen. In a sample of incomes gathered by the bureau of statistics from the 1941 census returns, it was found that 83-9 per cent of the wage earners of Canada received an income of less than $1,500. These people are not going to benefit very much from the exemption suggested, particularly on that part of the income which is over $1,500 or even $1,000. They will not benefit from the exemption because they do not receive the income. When you examine the various categories you find that wage earners receiving less than $500 a year numbered 1,028,800, or 35-9 per cent of the total wage earners in the country at that time. If these figures do not convince the members of this house that something should be done and done quickly to increase wages, I do not know what will convince them.
Another report to which hon. members may have seen, the Marsh report of 1941, gives the number of heads of families in certain income brackets.	City workers, heads of
families, earning from $500 to $1,000 a year, numbered 219.000 in 1941. Rural workers, heads of families, earning from $500 to $1,000 numbered 80,000. City workers, heads of families, earning $500 or less numbered 114,900. Rural workers, heads of families, earning $500 or less numbered 103,100. The year 1941 was a prosperous one. It was the year in which wages were frozen or stabilized, and in relation to the cost of living at this time wages are not much better, if any.
The government says that it considers it a fundamental principle to maintain, a high national income. A high national income cannot be maintained unless there is a high individual income* The two must go together.
I wish to make one other observation in connection with this $2,000 exemption from income tax. When the increase in the in-

demnity of hon. members was before us in the previous session I pointed out that as members of parliament we had not done anything to increase the standard of living of the people of this country. I could quote figures -I'have them here-to show that the amount of money being paid in wages has been continually falling since that time. Now that we have increased our own indemnities we are in duty bound n6t only to raise the exemption on income tax up to $2,000, but to see, as far as it lies with us, that every family receive an income of $2,000.
I should like to say a word in connection with a national labour code. The idea is not a new one to the group with which I am associated. We advocated it in our first manifesto in 1933, and we are still satisfied that it is a good thing. It is not only a good thing but an essential in harmonizing and stabilizing labour relations across the country. I am aware of the many difficulties, but I believe that P.C. 1003, faulty as it is, was a step in the right direction, that we should take advantage of its acceptance during war time, and that the government should do everything possible, even to the extent of an amendment of the British North America Act if agreement can be had to that end, to bring about conditions under which a national labour code will be part of the law's of Canada. In my opinion a labour code should set down minimum standards above which the provinces would be free to go, if they wished, but not free to go below.
I listened with much interest to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) on Monday of this week. It was a long speech, but in my opinion the most striking feature of it was that he spoke on both sides of almost every point he raised. He reminded me of the Roman god Janus who, I believe, was supposed to be the porter of heaven and the guardian deity of the gates. And, because of that, as a gate has two sides, he is usually shown with two heads.
The leader of the opposition referred to the fact-and it is a fact-that the housing situation in Canada is a festering sore on the body politic, and a national emergency. Then he went on to say-
During the war we met the national emergency courageously and forthrightly. Surely we shall not be less resolute in peace.
One or two pages further on in his speech he is reported in this way:
I do not urge the government to engage in rash efforts of decontrol, hut I do urge the government to prepare and make public, now that the war is over, a planned .programme to .relax, wage controls on low-wage people and .to free the productive processes of the country from the effects of those laws against production, which

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
were made necessary in war, but which in time of peace discouraged what is most essential to the production of needed /goods.
Well, I should not be a bit surprised if the government, without being over-rash, did come forward with a planned programme to relax controls, but I am fairly sure they will not have a planned programme for anything else.
The point I wish to make is this, we dealt with the national emergency courageously and forthrightly in war time, not by leaving things to people to do or not to do as they pleased, but by meeting the needs of war with all the power of the Canadian government and resources of the Canadian people. There is no other way in which we can deal with the housing emergency-no other than by meeting it with the whole power and resources of the Canadian people.
Referring to Canada's loan of $1,250 million to Great Britain, the hon. gentleman said, as reported at page 30:
From the point of view of the selfish interests of Canada, the loan is amply justified.
But on page 31 I find this:
But we might as well understand what we are doing . . . What this loan in fact means is that for five years the Canadian taxpayer will pay interest on ft which, even at 2J per cent, will be $30 million a year, and at the same rate on the extension of the 1942 interest-free loan te will pay $14 million.
I submit that if the loan is a good thing, and I agree that it is, it was proper that it should have been made. It is a good thing for Canada economically. I am convinced it it a good thing for the world and for Canada politically, and if we need to bring in humane considerations, I would say it is a good thing from the humane point of view. If we want to get a picture of the difference between what war did to Canada and what if did to Great Britain and Europe, we see it in the fact that this country can now lend $1,250 million to Great Britain, and that Great Britain needs such a loan. Nothing could show more clearly what the British people sacrificed in the war. I am in favour of going as far as possible to carry out our share of the war's costs, and I am convinced that anything we can do to help Britain now is a part of it.
A little further on the leader of the opposition referred to cartels and the control these institutions were gathering to themselves over production and other factors in our economy. I agree that cartels are gaining control of the economy of this country; but I do not agree that the government can eliminate the danger or menace of cartels by completely eliminating controls, and leaving everything to free enterprise. The purpose of every competitive organization, or every organization that is
supposed to be competitive, is to eliminate competition in its own line. I imagine no living organism of any kind likes competition, because competition makes living more difficult.
Let me read from the press release issued at the time the report on cartels was made public. It will give the house an idea of what cartels are doing to our economy and to our freedom; and then let anyone tell me how we are going to overcome this power by lessening the controls we now have over the economy of the country. The press release, under the heading "Economic effects of cartels", states:
The report discloses that in the two decades between world war I and world war II restrictive trade agreements of private interests flourished and spread; and that in so doing they (a) limited production and impeded the most efficient use of world resources; (b) raised or maintained certain consumer prices; (c) restricted the import and export of certain commodities; (d) restricted the use to which certain commodities might he put; (e) nullified external trade policies in certain respects; (f) resisted technological advances in certain fields; (g) created patent pools or monopolies covering wide fields of endeavour; (h) assisted the formation of private industrial empires which tended to supplant governments in the determination of certain national commercial policies.
In view of that statement by this Canadian commission which investigated cartels, how can anyone in this house or anywhere else say that the salvation of the people of Canada lies in giving free enterprise more control and more opportunity to do this sort of thing?
At the beginning of his address the leader of the opposition made this amazing statement.

The Address-Mr. Fleming

have the necessary power and control over the economy of the country to enable them to do so. I do not think it can carry out its responsibilities if it leaves the control in the hands of others. I suggest it is not fair to assert, on the one hand, that the government is responsible for the economic welfare of the individual, and to urge in the next breath that in connection with the economy of the country the productive forces be handed over to private individuals to operate them for their own profit. That is what my hon. friends to my right are advocating. I do not think even the leader of the opposition can ride two horses going in different directions. ,
The party with which I am associated agrees that the government has a responsibility for the social welfare of the people. At the same time we assert that the government can discharge that responsibility only when the productive forces of the country are used solely for the benefit of the people. This means planning; this means control. But it also means freedom-freedom from fear, freedom from want, and the assurance that the harder we work, the more secure we will be; not, as it is to-day, the realization that the harder we work the sooner we will be looking for another job.

I have referred to the constructive contribution made to this debate by my leader. There are two speeches to which I shall draw the
attention of the house, that of the Prime Minister and that of the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe). I suggest with all respect to these two hon. gentlemen that their contributions to the debate on the subject of housing were marked by smugness, complacency, boastfulness ar J an attempt to treat the whole subject in a trivial way. What we did not find in their speeches was realism. There was no courageous facing up to the problem which housing presents in Canada in its full dimensions or any indication that there would be a gearing of a great national effort to meet it. I am sorry that the Minister of Reconstruction is not in the house at the moment. I should like to say, as I have told him personally, and I believe in this I speak for all members, that we are delighted that he has returned from his vacation looking so much improved in health following the long-deferred vacation that he took between sessions, and we all hope that he will enjoy good health from it. At least his vacation has had a tonic effect upon his spirits, for if ever a man was full of optimism it was certainly the Minister of Reconstruction when he spoke in this debate two days .ago. He saw everything through rose-coloured glasses, and in listening to his speech and to that of the Prime Minister two days earlier I began to wonder if I was really living in the same country as they, because the descriptions that they gave of conditions as they seemed to find them were so utterly different from the actual conditions that I have seen that I had to pinch myself to see if I was really sitting here in this month of March in the Dominion of Canada. Their descriptions were of a very different kind of Canada from what I have seen in recent months.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, let us have a frank approach to and a clear appreciation of the immensity of this housing problem, and then let us view it in the light of the government's policy to meet it. The government has not met the housing problem. It has not taken adequate measures to cope with it. I wish that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Reconstruction would come to some of the places I have seen where men and women and their families, many of them veterans who have given long years of service to their country in this war, are living in hovels, garrets or cellar basements-not just one case but in thousands.
How big is this housing problem, Mr. Speaker? It is an immense problem. It has
The Address-Mr. Fleming

reached enormous proportions. Mr. Storms, general manager of Housing Enterprises Limited, said in a published statement on March 14 last that there are 375,000 families in Canada who ase involuntarily doubled up because of the housing shortage. Imagine-
375,000	families! That means almost 2,000,000 people. He went on to say that the situation was daily becoming worse with the arrival of soldiers and their dependents from overseas. It is a problem that mounts with every boatload of soldiers coming back from overseas. In the city of Toronto the authorities, who are doing their best to cope with local conditions, estimate that one-half of the discharged ex-servicemen want housing, and the problem is growing daily. The department of welfare of the city of Toronto keeps a record of the families who apply to them for housing accommodation, and in the last three months the number of unfilled applications on hand has increased by eighteen per cent. It has gone up'every week. The need is constantly growing. The situation is going to continue to grow wrnrse if we can expect nothing more from the government than has been indicated hitherto in this debate. It would be cruel to mislead the people of Canada into thinking that with the kind of programme the government has indicated conditions can improve.
It is a bitterly cruel fact that those who are bearing the brunt of the housing shortage in Canada to-day are our veterans. After long years of separation from their wives and families, tens of thousands of them have come back to find themselves either still separated from their families or having to double up under intolerable conditions. The readjustment period will be difficult enough for many of these men without their having to face all that may be involved in domestic conditions in the present intolerable situation. As Mr. Storms pointed out, the problem is going to become increasingly acute with the arrival from overseas of the soldiers and the dependents of those who have married overseas. The hon. member who seconded the address (Mr. Winters) had this to say as reported at page 19 of Hansard:
We do not overlook the fact that many of our soldiers are bringing war brides and families with them to Canada, and we wish to assure them of a welcome in this country.
But it will be a very sad welcome indeed that many thousands of these wives are going to receive in Canada in having to submit to the doubling up which will be necessary if they are to have a roof over their heads. There will be more of them living in cellars and garrets.

We have had intolerable conditions in other respects as well. I have already referred to the unequal burden borne by the veterans, and I should like to make mention also of the very unequal share of the burden that is being borne by people with families. Unless the government in framing its housing plans for the future takes into account the claims of people with families and puts them first after the claims of the ex-service personnel we are going to leave a crying social need unsolved.
There are other problems, too. I have personal knowledge of two cases in Montreal which were brought to my attention, and which are only typical of many others, showing the methods being practised to evade the rent control regulations. In one case the rent paid was the rent fixed by the rental authority, but the sum of $500 was exacted from the tenant for the purchase of the key. In another case an apartment had been rented furnished, but the prospective tenant was compelled to buy the furniture at an utterly exorbitant price. Astute minds have been directed to devising methods of defeating the rent control regulations.
The effect has been very unhappy indeed on the reestablishment of veterans. One reason why so many of the ex-service men have not yet found employment is that they have been kept so busy trying to find housing accommodation they have not had time or opportunity or perhaps the will to look about for needed employment. That condition is common all over Canada, and particularly in-the large cities. It is retarding recovery on the employment side, the reconversion side. You will find it acute in mining communities and in logging communities. There is a great-need of proper housing accommodation adjacent to the big camps in many great logging areas in this country, not only in the east but in the west, in British Columbia, on Vancouver island and elsewhere.
The suggestion has been made by someone: Oh, let the surplus people in the cities go to the farms. But so long as we have these glowingly optimistic statements from the Minister of Reconstruction about the great opportunities of employment and high wages which will be available in industry you will not find many people going back from the large cities to the rural areas from which many of them came. Conditions are so bad that in some cities there has been interference with the law; but it is a great tribute to the law-abiding character of our people that under conditions of great stress there has been so little lawlessness over present housing condi-

tions. In some communities, however, there has been interference with sheriffs to prevent evictions of ex-service personnel. The government must take account of this situation.
What have been the activities of the government in this field? Well, we hatl a statement given to the press by the Minister of Reconstruction-hon. members will find it in the *Ottawa Journal of February 11-which is a pretty fair sample of what happens when you get three ministers in the same administration competing for power in connection with housing matters or any others. Wartime Housing is the only department of government that is doing anything to get thepe houses built.
The only department! Well, I will accept his confession as applied to the other departments of government.
What is this great record of Wartime Housing Limited of which the Minister of Reconstruction boasts? I will give the house one experience. It is the experience that the city of Toronto had with contracts for 603 houses to be built in adjacent communities. These were to be semi-permanent houses. Unfortunately, Wartime Housing Limited decided that, of the 7,000 houses that it laid down in its 1945 programme, 6,200 were to be built without cellars, and only 800 with cellars. Under these conditions the city of Toronto had to take these houses without [DOT]cellars; and what is the result? The first sod was turned on July 4, 1945, and a very optimistic statement-of course statements which [DOT]come from the government or its minions are always optimistic-came from the representative of Wartime Housing Limited on that occasion. A fine record indeed 1 Wartime Housing Limited is still going on, wherever distracted municipalities apply for help, exacting harsh terms. They are still demanding a free gift of the best sites from the municipalities ; they are still demanding subsidies in the form of donations of land and low taxes. Wartime Housing is still going on disturbing the normal channels of distribution by its high-handed requisitioning methods.
What is the situation in respect of building materials? We have a glowing account in the throne speech of what is to be done to provide building materials, and we have this remarkable statement of the Minister of Reconstruction as quoted in the Ottawa Journal of February 11:
We have beaten the shortage of brick, and lumber is now coming on the market in good quantities for houses.
Hon. members will remember, too, that he said in the house on the 20th of this month that perhaps lumber was the least of our problems and that, generally speaking, the situation was well in hand. I do not know what the Minister of Reconstruction means when he says that the problem of brick has been beaten, and that lumber is coming on the market in large quantities. It just does not fit the facts as the supply houses in the country know them. It does not fit the facts as they exist in Toronto and the other big cities of Canada. Talk about beating the situation in brick! One of the building materials which is in most critically short supply is brick; if there is another in the same category it is lumber; and it is not good enough to have these glowingly optimistic statements from the Minister of Reconstruction when they cannot be supported by facts. I will not take time to review the glowing statement made on that occasion. But the house will recall this, that

We do not ask the impossible of the government, but we want a frank facing up to this situation. In large measure we lay the responsibility for this problem at the doorstep of the government. Why cannot we- recognize it in ours? I speak now of the government and of parliament. I thank the house for its great courtesy. I promise hon. members I shall be brief. When President Truman gave instructions to Mr. Wilson Wyatt, his housing administrator, now housing expediter, to draft a plan for the United States he gave him only one instruction and it was this, "Make no little plans." the 1946 programme of the government in the field of construction. If it has a 1946 programme or objective it still remains a profound secret so far as this house is concerned. We must have a goal. That is rental housing. That is a drop in the bucket. Let us not delude ourselves that this will be low-rent housing. It cannot be. The cost of construction to-day is such that Housing Enterprises Limited cannot build low-rent housing as that term is properly understood. They will probably be medium-rental houses.
Let us have a proper understanding of what is involved, I am not going to go over the promiseS that the government and its supporters made in the last election campaign. The house will remember the promises of the
600.000	to 1,000,000 houses. Let us see the big plan. We have not heard about it in parliament. Let us have the big bold plan they advertised in the campaign. Where is it? We in this house would like to see the government's big bold plan

The year 1946 marks a troubled era in the history of the world. The war came to an end last year; still, all nations feel that peace has not yet returned. While the great powers are endeavouring to ensure it through an agreement based upon the respect of treaties and mutual confidence, the nations, great or small, are making a determined effort with a view to reestablishing their upset economy. Each country, in the turmoil of the post-war period, seeks practical solutions, works out the most diversified plans, but faces the future not without some fears that the circumstances justify.
Canada, like the other nations, must now solve internal problems which are both serious and complicated. They crop up so fast and in such numbers that the government, unable to solve them all at once, must perforce concentrate on the most pressing ones.
.1 recognize that such a situation is disquieting to them; besides, it is depressing for the people who, now that war is over, are anxious

to enjoy peace and who, not finding it up to their expectations, voice their resentment in no uncertain terms.
Discontent is rife among the people. It is kindled less by democracy than by its occasional abuse, less by wealth than by its frequent abuse, less by our recognized laws than by their oft-neglected implementation. To our other evils, war has added excessive legislation which the people accepted as a necessary consequence of the armed conflict. To this legislation, hundreds of orders of all sorts were grafted, many of which smacked so obviously of sheer experiment, contrivance and artificiality that on the whole, they could not be favourably accepted. As a result, our democratic system is beginning to feel the repercussions of this discontent. "War is over, say the people. Then, why is such and such a policy still in effect? Why is such another preserved?" Dissatisfaction is intensified by the fact that while hostilities lasted, the praises of peace were sung far and wide and we were promised that the end of the war would bring about universal comfort and happiness. However, reality with its sad disillusions has kindled all over, but especially among the working classes a feeling of discontent which tends to become sharper. The piling up of insignificant causes inevitably brings about tremendous results. Unimportant facts, harmless if isolated, are sooner or later directed to some definite goal. Unconsciously or otherwise, they generate certain trends which, though weak at first gather more and more impetus and finally become overwhelming. Such trends are at present influencing our national life and current events are causing deep concern among the masses who are becoming impatient. Can you blame the people, driven to distraction by excessive legislation and generosity, subjected to all sorts of restrictions and witnessing the extravagant methods of capital, for still believing in happiness, and wishing for comfort, work and a home while at the same time pressing for security?	.
To live an honest and happy life, a minimum of comfort and well-being is needed. If that is lacking, if people are deprived of work, home, food and clothing, the door is wide open to the most dangerous abuses. Whenever a member of the national family, no longer believing in the democratic system, leans towards socialism seeing in this doctrine a remedy to all the evils he suffers at the hands of more fortunate individuals, another cell disintegrates and disappears. Since the end of the war, trends of thought-there is no need to specify-'have taken shape and expanded. Unemployment has given rise to them. If we wish to insure the security of

The people have been made to pay exceedingly heavy taxes; we have had an income tax applying both to/capital and savings. Those taxes have cut into the capital of the citizens with a fixed income; they have cut into the capital of manufacturers who have to meet obligations incurred before the war; today, unable to obtain raw materials, they no longer have, once their taxes are paid, the funds necessary for the modernization of their plants.

We are now at peace and yet, in the name of peace, we are asking Canada to lend money and contribute to loans which will add, in capital and interest, to the already heavy burden resting on our shoulders.
During the war I objected to such generosity. When the bill covering the $1,250 million comes before the house for approval, I reserve the right to define my attitude in the light of the information given and express my full views on the matter. At this stage of our national life, when our debt has increased from 63260-13
$4 to $16 billion in five years, we should not become overexcited but should tackle the problem of reforming our eoonomy.

We have helped them and are still doing so with pride as well as generosity. These are the causes of dissatisfaction among the people. Mingle with them and you will be convinced. Among veterans, there is more grumbling than we think. However, its application has become absolutely impossible in many parts of Canada. Why? Other groups of citizens are also dissatisfied and crave a little more justice $nd attention. Failure of the government to forecast, in the speech from the throne, any relief whatever from our present tax set-up has been a source of great disappointment. Lower taxes would offer relief to industrialists, merchants, civil servants, farmers, heads of

On the other hand, I claim that it is unfair to keep in detention or in camps, farm labourers or skilled employees, as, for example, expert buttermakers when the scarcity of butter is so pronounced, or lumbermen, when they are so urgently needed in the bush, or again, electricians and skilled carpenters when the building trade is paralyzed. The speech from the throne forecasts the immediate implementation of measures directed at maintaining employment at a high level and solving the extremely acute housing problem. These are both urgent legislations. I welcome them and so do the Canadian

people who are clamouring for them. I shall support the address, as a token of my appreciation for those two pieces of legislation, but, as I said before, I shall reserve the right to vote according to my views on the bill concerning the billion and a quarter loan on which, no doubt, the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) will give us full particulars.
The housing situation is critical. I believe it is in our own interest to see that ou-r markets are supplied with sufficient building materials; then it might be justifiable to ship our surplus overseas. In this field, as in others, there is no reason why foreigners should be supplied before our own people.
Employment is the means of supplying work. A nation cannot be happy when unemployment is prevalent. Prior to 1939, the undertaking of public works was urged; however, under pretense of curtailing expenses, they were denied. Then war was declared and millions .were juggled around. To wage and win the war, billions of dollars were instantly available. Could we now refuse to earmark a few hundred million dollars each year to fight unemployment through the country, applying them to the undertaking of public works that would remain an asset for Canada? To ensure peace, maintain the democratic prestige of our country, prevent our population from subscribing to subversive doctrines, attain true national security, work is the essential factor.
I shall not support the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). It evidences a lack of sincerity which is characteristic of the party he directs. I fail to understand that it now stands for economies and reductions in taxes, since, during the war years, government expenditures were never large enough in its opinion. The Conservative party does not enjoy public confidence; even under its new camouflage, it has not been successful in overcoming the sorry reputation it acquired during the first Great War. On this side of the house freedom of speech is a reality; we may frankly utter our thoughts, even if they are at variance with those of our colleagues. This makes for strength in the ranks of the Liberals. Our party is not based on egotism, coercion, blind subservience to an official platform or a "believe or die" policy; it will survive when all others have collapsed, for no other party has recognized to a fuller extent the value of individuality and freedom.
I shall not support the sub-amendment of the C.C.F. party. I rely too much on private enterprise to subscribe to a socialist doctrine *which, although moderate, must still be contrary to the best interests of a country like Canada. The war years, due to the amount of

The Address-Mr. LaCroix
work they have provided, have deprived socialism of its best opportunities. As I said before, so that this theory, with others similar to it, may have no chance of spreading, work is absolutely necessary.
Social security in all fields: food in the larder of every home, ownership of property made easy for all, hardship eliminated, social evils suppressed, maximum encouragement given to agriculture, private enterprise fostered, youth assisted and encouraged, happiness everywhere: that is the part the government should1 play in 1046 and in subsequent years. They have accomplished a tremendous task during the war. Why could they not do as much in peace time? Canada occupies an important place among the nations of the world. However she must continue her activities in the fields of industry, commerce, agriculture, mining, forestry, and in all other national spheres. Her future is in her own hands. The other nations, intent on solving their own problems, will not help her to reestablish herself and, in the field of business, where gratitude is frequently unknown, the nations including Great Britain will never surrender the freedom which they have always held of buying wherever they see fit. Therefore, it is Canada's duty, in the name of the elementary principle of self-preservation, not to exceed the limits of common sense. Will Canada have won the peace if within her own borders there are unemployment, dislocation and discouragement? First and above all, we must prevent the evil of unemployment. In addition, we must lighten the burden borne by the workers and others in the lower salary brackets and develop further throughout the country the program of social security which has been so successfully launched by the present government. We have reached a decisive hour when every Canadian must become a crusader in order to protect and defend the social structure against trouble-makers, against promoters of ideas which are inconsistent with our parliamentary system and our Christian traditions. That which fosters unity within a nation is the joy which everyone feels in belonging to such a nation. Social security and national security are two words which are inseparable and which are guarantees for the future. By keeping them to the fore, by uniting them, by blending them, we shall make Canada a healthy, united and powerful country.

No one more than I desires the independence of my country, but I wish to attain this object by orderly and legitimate means.
, Patriotism is instilled not by resorting to bloodshed but by winning over the hearts and minds of people. History shows ,that all those who have attained power or achieved their aims [DOT]through violence have been forcibly brought down from the pinnacle on which they had ensconsed themselves.
We can reply to advocates of revolutionary communism and nationalism by striving to improve our social legislation for the benefit of the public, by firmly repressing monopolies and by passing laws which, economically speaking, will allow a better distribution of the national wealth. Now that we have accomplished a tremendous war effort, far beyond our means, sound patriotism must include a generous thought for our own citizens to whom we should grant relief from taxation as rapidly as possible to enable them readily to attain a normal social balance.
Hence I deem it my duty to protest forthwith against those periodical gifts to England, the brunt of which will be borne by the majority of our citizens. I have a great respect for the British commonwealth of nations, but as you know, sir, I have always felt that a Canadian worthy of the name, who has pledged allegiance to his country and must serve its interests first and foremost, should protect the public treasury against those who are prone to make gifts to other nations which, in many instances, are wealthier than we are.
Ireland safeguarded her own interests during the war. No one holds any grudge against her and her prestige has not declined anywhere in the world.
I respect the views of those who differ with me in regard to the meaning of the words "to serve one's country", but I deemed it my duty to vote against participation and against each billion dollar gift which, under one form or another, we have so generously made during the war. I have at the time stated the reasons for my stand and, in my opinion, [DOT]those reasons still hold to-day.
From a strictly Canadian point of view, I believe that this further loan of SI ,250 million, Which will not bear any interest for five years, is not a good business proposition for our country, because this agreement which I have read most carefully, contains no provision compelling England to spend this money in Canada. England, whose memory is short where Canada's efforts on her behalf are concerned, does not, under this agreement, undertake to lift the restrictions she has imposed on Canadian products, not only within her own borders but all over the sterling area. England 
will be able to spend our Canadian dollars anywhere and in any way she sees fit in order to rebuild her pre-war economy. Whenever it suits her purpose, England can even continue do purchase wheat from the Argentine rather than from Canada, or give prefer-ance to Denmark's bacon over our own farm produce, and experience has taught me that the dictates of her interests will be the sole guide in the matter.
In short, Canadians will not only have helped England win the war, but also assist her in her, conquest of world markets. Our dollar will serve as Great Britain's ambassador. Since we export 40 per cent of our production, we shall help to impair our own markets, while ostensibly attempting to maintain England's; for, if she spends our dollars elsewhere, Great Britain will insist that the countries whose goods she purchases reciprocates with certain privileges. These will certainly not be to our advantage, and we shall recover our funds through banking transactions rather than through the sale of our goods.
It may be claimed that at the present time Great Britain has tremendous contracts in Canada and that the loan will help to pay for them. No mention is made of these contracts, however, in the terms of the agreement between Great Britain and Canada, and there is nothing to prevent England from cancelling them if she can do better business elsewhere.
The British are business men. Far from hating them, I admire them, but I sincerely wish we had, as members of the Canadian government, men with as much business sense as they possess.
Australia refused a loan to England and I fail to see why we should be an easier prey than the Australians. I much prefer, in Europe, Great Britain's influence to that of Russia, but I do not think it necessary to drain our coffers to attain that end. The loan and gifts we are making under this agreement are five times greater than the loan to Great Britain contemplated by the United States, in proportion to the respective populations of the two countries. Are we wealthier than the Americans? Are our anticipated revenues superior to those of the United States and England? I do not think so.
I beg to denounce with the greatest energy the condescension and lack of Canadian spirit evidenced by the leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), who blamed the other nations of the commonwealth for failing to grant loans to England and who stated, as reported in Hansard of March 19, 1946:
I think the loan should have been made to Great Britain interest free.

Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne made no reference to several matters which to me appear to be of paramount importance to most Canadians. For instance, the citizens of my province will be particularly disappointed that the speech contains no proposal to commence any major irrigation projects in Saskatchewan during the current year. I raise the matter at this time, because in the constituency of Moose Jaw the shortage of water, which has plagued us for decades, has recently become dangerously acute.
As most hon. members know, the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina are located in the semi-arid section of the prairies. These two centres with a total population of approximately 80,000 people are almost entirely dependent for their water supplies on underground water and wells. For forty years, or ever since Moose Jaw became a city, the authorities have had trouble giving the people a twenty-four hour supply of water the year round. I have seen people in Moose Jaw

The Address-Mr. Thatcher
plant lawns and gardens in the spring, only to see them die later in the year because the city authorities were forced to shut off the water or ration it.
Several years ago the federal government, realizing the gravity of the situation, sought to alleviate it by building a pumping station and reservoir near Riverhurst on the South Saskatchewan river. From there an open ditch about seventy miles long was constructed to a point near Moose Jaw. That open ditch did help the situation somewhat, and we were grateful for it, but on the whole it has proved inadequate.
Since the first of the year the water situation in Moose Jaw has been worse than at any time in the history of the city. The day I left Moose Jaw to come to Ottawa the water-mains were closed for about twelve hours. That situation prevailed during most of February and part of January. I ask hon. members to try to realize what it means to a city of 25,000 to have the water-mains shut off for part of the day. This winter, housewives were forced to fill their bathtubs the night before, if they wanted to have water to cook during the day time. Sanitary facilities could not be used while the water was cut off. Several times when I got up in the morning I could not shave because I had forgotten to put water aside the night before.
During February several of our major industries which use large quantities of water had to close down.for several days at a time, and during that period hundreds of men were unemployed. Moose Jaw is the main divisional point of the Canadian Pacific railway in Saskatchewan. We had the spectacle this winter of the railroad bringing in trainloads of tank cars filled with water to keep their trains running across the prairies. On top of all this the city authorities are worried over the health aspect. When the water-mains have been closed down for ten or twelve hours and the water finally comes, it is a rusty colour and apparently filled with foreign material. I mention these facts simply to give hon. members some idea of the magnitude of the water problem that the city of Moose Jaw is facing to-day.
The city of Regina is in a somewhat similar position. It has been a little more fortunate than Moose Jaw up to the present, but to-day Regina, with its growing population, is also finding that the demand for water is exceeding the supply. An article appeared in the Regina Leader-Post of September 15 last, headed "city near limit of water supply," which reads in part:
"Regina has pretty well reached the limit of her present water supply," J. W. D. Farrel, waterworks superintendent, said Friday.
Deep artesian wells from which the city has been taking its water give between 5,500,000 and 6,000,000 gallons a day on the average. This summer the city could have used 7,000,000 gallons a day, if the quantity had been available.
The city of Weyburn also has experienced grave water shortages over the past few years. In other words, the future growth and industrial development of these three prairie cities is almost completely dependent on their obtaining an adequate water supply. Indeed, if new supplies of water are not obtained they may have great difficulty in maintaining their present population.
The problem of obtaining water for these cities is tied up in an integral way with obtaining a larger amount of water for the farm lands of that part of Saskatchewan. As hon. members know, our farmers in that area have fought drought conditions for many years. On the prairies water is liquid gold. Yet, despite our great need for that liquid gold, we as a people are to-day letting vast quantities pass under our noses without using it in Saskatchewan.
What is the solution? Every Canadian I think knows of the mighty rivers that have their source in the Rocky mountains and flow across the prairies into Hudson bay. But perhaps many do not realize how little we are using these rivers to-day. There is very little navigation, not a great deal of irrigation, and very little hydro-electrical development.
One of these rivers flows about eighty miles northwest of Moose Jaw. When one reads of the immense dams that have been built in so-called backward nations such as India, China, Egypt, Spain, and others, for irrigation purposes, one cannot help wondering why we have for so long neglected to water our burning plains and why our major Saskatchewan cities must be so short of water. For many years the people of Saskatchewan have urged the building of a huge dam northwest of Moose Jaw. This proposed project has been called the South Saskatchewan power and irrigation scheme. It would involve the construction of a daw near Elbow.
The project would have three main purposes: (1) The providing of an abundant supply of water for domestic and industrial use for the two largest cities in the southern part of the province, Regina and Moose Jaw; (2) the development of hydro-electric energy; (3) the irrigation of several hundred thousand acres of land in that area.
Is this scheme feasible? Permit me to quote from an address by Mr. E. L. Gray, of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration, to agricultural representatives from all parts of the province gathered in Regina on February

The Address-Mr. Thatcher

19 of this year. He is reported to have said:
Construction of a dam on the South Saskatchewan river near Elbow as the huh of a great power and irrigation scheme is considered feasible.
Extensive drilling and surveys by the prairie farm rehabilitation administration bad located a site where a giant dam could be built at the upper reaches of the Qu'Appelle and Saskatchewan rivers near Elbow.
Mr. A. W. E. Fawkes, Moose Jaw city engineer, in 1933 recommended the construction of such a dam. In his opinion the construction of a dam about 200 feet high to impound the waters of the South Saskatchewan is quite feasible, and the stored water would be capable of irrigating somewhere in the neighbourhood of 500,000 acres. Other authorities have made similar statements.
In Alberta water resources have been harnessed to the service of the people. Huge areas which were formerly useless because of lack of water, are to-day called the gardens of the west. Certain sections of the United States have been even more successful in irrigating dry lands. There is no reason why what has been done in Alberta and the United States cannot be done in Saskatchewan.
This scheme, if proceeded with, would have seven major advantages not only for the people of Saskatchewan but for the people of Canada as a whole:
1.	It would provide a permanent water supply for Regina, Moose Jaw and many smaller centres, for both domestic and industrial use.
2.	It would make possible a considerable development of hydro electric power.
3.	It would permit the irrigation of several hundred thousand acres of fertile farm land.
4.	Its actual construction at the present time or in thfe near future would provide jobs for many unemployed in that district who are to-day without work.
5.	The project would permit considerable industrial development such as canning factories and sugar beet factories which, in turn, would employ many returned men.
6.	The project would permit the stabilization of agriculture in that area by (a) the control of moisture and (b) allowing a diversification of crops.
7.	Finally, I would suggest that the project would act as an insurance throughout the area against future heavy relief costs such as we had in the depression years.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the government must favour the scheme because during the last federal election, government spokesmen stated definitely that the project would be completed. May I be permitted to quote from an advertisement which appeared in the Moose Jaw Times of Saturday, June 9 last:

The South Saskatchewan Thunder creek irrigation programme alone will undoubtedly contribute much to the prosperity of the city and [DOT] surrounding district. This project will be commenced immediately men and materials are available. ... It has been approved.
Both the men and the materials are, I believe, now available, or, if not, they soon will be available, and we ask that the government proceed in accordance with its promise.
During the past winter months the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) did some very fine work in focussing the attention of easterners on the urgent need for irrigation in western Canada. Every westerner is grateful to him for his efforts. The seriousness of this problem makes it essential that all political parties lend their support to it.
Since coming to Ottawa I have seen parliament lend or give away hundreds of millions of dollars to other nations. Surely we are not asking too much when we ask that the government spend a few million dollars on our own people and in the development of our own country. The South Saskatchewan river project would prove to be one of the finest investments that the government of Canada ever made. It would pay for itself in a relatively short period of time. I respectfully urge the government to include the scheme in this year's estimates and to proceed with its construction without delay.

It may interest you, Mr. Speaker, and the house, when I tell you that I am in rather a unique position. If I followed the wish of the electors who sent me here I should spend half my time sitting on the other side of the house and half over here. I was sent here by Liberal and Conservative electors who preferred to elect a representative of one of the old standard parties rather than one of the new sort. One reason why I have not gone over there was that I have not been invited, and the other is that if I ever did go I do not think I would be able to come back here-
You would not want to.
-so that I think I will stay where I am. In all the years I have been in politics-and I was first elected to this house in 1921, before quite a number of hon. members were born
Oh, oh.

-and in all the parliaments of which I have been a member, I believe I have had a seat on the Speaker's left, except in one parliament, in which I was

The Address-Mr. Black (Yukon)
fortunate, or perhaps unfortunate, enough to occupy the position, Mr. Speaker, which you do now. I tried to be neutral. Perhaps I had a more difficult task than your Honour has, for you never had to find your own Prime Minister out of order, which on one occasion I was forced to do; but that only added interest and perhaps difficulty to the position. T will say this as a former Speaker, that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) treated me when I was Speaker with the utmost courtesy and consideration, as much so as though I had been his own choice for the Speakership.
My policy as a member of parliament has been to support, regardless of party, legislation which I believed was in the best interest of Canada, and that is what I intend to continue to do.
Perhaps this is rather personal, but forty-eight years ago this month I went to Yukon with the great gold rush of that day. I did not intend to live there. Like thousands of other young men, I expected to pick up a fortune in the gold mines in a couple of years and, as they say up there, come "outside" to live. To a Yukoner anywhere but Yukon, whether it be the United States, or Canada, or South America, is "outside." However, I found out that I could get along better by letting miners do my mining than by trying myself to mine, that I was better fitted to my own profession, and I went back to it and stayed with it. In 1896, fifty years ago, Dawson City was born; and I ask hon. members who know anything about mining how many mining camps in the world have lasted over fifty years and are still going strong, which is the case in Yukon. Yukon has produced approximately 1300 million in gold and millions of dollars worth of silver, lead and zinc; and I predict- and I think I know what I am talking about -that fifty years hence we shall still be producing those precious metals in Yukon.
Some people have the idea that Yukon has been just a bill of expense to Canada; but if an account were taken of the royalties paid to the government on gold mined-and mind you, the royalties first charged on gold mined in Yukon were ten per cent of the output, then reduced to 'five per cent, and now 2J per cent, and that runs into money-and when one stops to think that almost everything we use in the way of food, clothing, machinery, tools and equipment; of all kinds is imported, it may be realized what a market it has provided for Canada, and what a large amount of money has been paid on customs duties on imported goods. Yukon does not get much credit for that, because most of the 63260-144
duties are paid at the ports of Vancouver, Edmonton and Victoria, but it is Yukoners who pay the bill.
During the war, mining in Yukon, as in the whole of North America, was practically suspended. Nearly all the young men of war age joined the army, the navy and the air force and went out to do their duty. By international consent the United States army came into northern Canada and in the common cause built war projects. Fortunately the exigencies of war did not require the use in conflict of most of these projects, and they remain to-day assets of Canada. On April 3 next the responsibility of maintaining the Alaska highway will be turned over from the army of the United States to the army of Canada. I hope our government and army will never consider for one moment allowing that road to go back to bush. It is too important a highway. It is not located where the international commission, appointed three years before the war to advise their respective United States and Canadian governments, would have recommended that the road should be built, but it was put through in a rush by the United States army, with our help, and it is a wonderful asset to Canada. Without expense to us it was built with United States money and labour, and already it has made accessible in Yukon and in northern British Columbia parts of the country which formerly were almost inaccessible. Prospectors going in there to look for minerals would take about a year to get in and they would go with pack horses and canoes and pack loads on their own backs. Now they can use the road and in a few days or hours make their camp and prospect in the vicinity. That, if nothing else, is what the road is now being used for.
Among other projects which the United , States undertook and completed in northern Canada through northern British Columbia was a wonderful telephone system from Prince Rupert, on the coast, to all the interior small settlements. I hope that the governments of Canada and of British Columbia will, in their wisdom, maintain those telephone lines, not turn them over to War Assets Corporation, probably to be tossed into the lap of the monopoly known as the British Columbia Telephone Company, which would likely dismantle them and take the material into larger communities and use it there, and deprive the people in the outlying settlements of this means of communication. I hope the governments will maintain these lines and operate them.
Considering the great return which Yukon has given Canada in wealth, including levies
The Address-Mr. Mclvor

of various kinds, I feel justified in pointing out to the house, and in particular to the Ministers of Mines, of Finance, of Reconstruction, and of Public Works that Yukon to-day is suffering from lack of roads. Dawson City, the centre of that immense gold mining area, has no means of communication in winter except by plane; there is not a road into that town. The same thing is true of the centre of the wonderful silver mines, Mayo. In winter time they depend entirely on planes, and as hon. members know, the weather makes planes uncertain. In former times there were roads connecting both Dawson City and that silver camp with the coast, but they have been allowed to fall into disuse. A comparatively small amount of money would put them back into shape to use. For the immediate present I appeal to the Minister of Mines and to the cabinet to be generous even to a small degree and vote an amount of money that will put that road back in shape for trucking, not for joy riding but as a road that will carry trucks containing ore concentrates to the main artery of navigation on the Yukon river. This can be done for not more than $100,000; and what is that in these days when we are talking about and spending billions? Speaking on behalf of Yukon, I hope that we shall receive some consideration at the hands of the government.

Like the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), I will not attempt to make a speech; instead I will try to say something. I do not think any man has a right to stand up here unless he has something to say. Some great speeches have been made in this debate on all sides of the house, but I have one criticism to offer. When a man rises in his place and , makes a speech and you do not see him in the house until he comes back to make another speech, then I suggest that he is not making the best contribution to the debates of the house.
Congratulations are in order, but sometimes it happens that honours do not go to the right people, because I am convinced-it is not "I think" but "I know"-that there are men and women who are unknown one hundred miles from their homes and who nevertheless are the greatest heroes and heroines in our country by reason of their public service and of their sacrifices. Let me tell the house about one man. He was a missionary in China and was forced back home because of the war. His name is Duncan McRae. He took a church near Arnprior at White Lake. He is sixty-eight years of age and soon he will be on his way back to China. I say that man is

a hero, and yet he is nothing compared with his wife, who will leave her daughter and son and go back with him to the front line. That is something we are bound to admire. That man was the best athlete in Manitoba; there was no one who could touch him. I have seen him take seven firsts. He took the weights, the hurdles and the jumps. I must admit that I played a trick on him once when he was nearly beaten in the broad jump. He had put his handkerchief in the tracks of the man who preceded him, and when he turned his back I moved the handkerchief up a foot. He came tearing down and cleared the handkerchief. There was laughter and he turned to me and said, "What is the matter, Dan?" I said, "Nothing is the matter, but I should have it up another foot. I moved your handkerchief up another foot." He was an honour student and a great athlete, and yet he could give his life to the greatest calling on earth. He is a real hero.
I congratulate those, whoever they may be, who in handing out honours did not pass up a member of the clergy, when Major Foote, a Presbyterian minister, received the Victoria Cross for his heroism at Dieppe. I do not think there is anyone who has surpassed him in quiet heroism and courage. He had done everything he could and was wondering how soon he would be in kingdom come, but he survived, and as he saw his fellow soldiers being taken off to the prison camp he decided that he simply could not go back to a comfortable bed and home. He therefore joined them and went back to the prison camp with them. He served faithfully, and I congratulate the person responsible for extending to Major Foote the highest possible honour which a man can win on the battlefield.
I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on having the courage to take fifty per cent of the wheat out of the distilleries. I think that took courage, but I do not believe that there is in this house a man or woman, nor do I believe that outside this house there are men and women, who would not deny themselves their nightcap or eye-opener in order to give some hungry kid some shredded wheat and milk or no milk. I commend the Prime Minister, but I suggest that he might have done better. He might have taken it all and put it into food.
The Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) surprises me sometimes-

He surprises a lot of people.
Mr. McIVOR; -but he continues to be an optimist. Somebody says that one optimist is worth fifty pessimists, and after what the

The Address-Mr. Mclvor
Minister of Reconstruction has come through during the war years I do not think there is anyone who does not admire him. There is not a man in Canada who has dqne a better job and he has come through these war years an optimist. There was an election thrown into the bargain and there were pessimists who said he would not get elected; but he was as sure of being elected as I was, and perhaps a little more so. He came through that and now he has a right to be an optimist.
Let me give an example of reconversion. Take Canada Car in Fort William. He assisted them in more ways than one. When the strikes came in the United States and there were labour troubles, Canada Car had to shut down. I had an opportunity of visiting the managers and controllers, and I could see those telegrams, one after another, expressing regret that, owing to the strike, material could not be forwarded. I expect to see Canada Car humming before long. I have one criticism. I thought it should have kept going, making buses up to the point where they needed spare parts, but they did mot do so. However, when I saw the plant I was amazed. I was pretty well acquainted with it, and .1 could see those aeroplanes lined up the full length of the plant, each receiving a part and beihg pushed on closer to the point of success. Now there are buses, one after another, a splendid example of reconversion. I repeat, the minister has a right to be optimistic.
I also visited Steep Rock. I do not know much about it, nor does Canada know much about it, but ere long, Canada will know that we have one of the greatest hematite mines in the country, and it will be doing things.
I do not like to say anything about the spy trouble we have had in Canada because I am not a lawyer, nor have I a judicial mind, but I like to help anybody if I can, no matter what mistakes they make. If we do not make those mistakes, dear knows we may make others. If a man says he never made a mistake, then he is just lying like sam hill. I should like to take the verdict of the leader of the opposition in the upper house, a college mate of mine. He has good sound judgment even though he is a Conservative. He commends the government for their stand. He can afford to do so without speaking politically.
I wondered in my own little mind what would have happened if Germany had not attacked Russia. Russia might never have beep in the war, because neither the United States nor Great Britain would have attacked her. What we ought to have to-day is patience and Christian charity, because the Russian backgrqund is altogether different from ours.
I have no patience with any man who breaks his oath or lies in any way. He has no right to do so, but I was proud in this house when the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose) took his seat and nobody made any fuss over him, although of course, some of us looked that way. Tolerance is one of the things we need to practise.
We think of peace, but to me peace that leaves out the Peacemaker will never give us a permanent peace.' On the Sabbath day most of the members go to hear the story of the Prince of Peace-if you do not, you ought to-and yet when we come into this house and think of the economic system of our country we forget all about the Prince of Peace, because I am convinced that money and things in Canada and in the United States are in the saddle. It is the dollar yardstick.
I heard a man who came back from the San Francisco conference say that the hope of the united ' nations lay in social security and economics. Hon. members know whether they believe that or not; I do not. I have heard- I am using my own words now-of a premier of a province who said that the hope of the united nations lies in having a common store of supplies; and yet the Great Teacher with thundering emphasis said:
_ Btut seek ye first the kingdom of God, and His righteousness; and all these things shall ibe added unto you.
That is from Him who knows. A man next to Him in greatness in the New Testament said:
For other foundations can no man lay than that which is laid in Christ Jesus.
Offer social security, economics or dollars and you will go to the bow-wows sooner or later. That is not the finding of to-day; that is the finding of the history of every age since the world began.
I should like to encourage the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) just a little bit by saying that he should make sure that the Sabbath day is kept free from toil for every toiler. There are men in this 'house who remind me of the old commandment, "Remember the i Sabbath day to keep it holy". Then I am reminded of a play I saw which said that if you break the ten commandments the ten commandments will break you. You cannot break the law of God and not suffer from it. I would encourage the Minister of Labour to make sure that, now the war is over, during which time so many inroads were made upon the Sabbath day, corporations will give to men their day of rest whether they use it in one way or another. I could recommend to them how to use it.
