The rules of the house will be up for revision shortly. About seven years ago I circulated a petition in this house to have the acoustics improved. Hon. members are not as fortunate as I am. I have a hearing aid and I can hear far better than hon. members believe. I think the time has arrived when it will not be necessary for the Speaker to put his hand to his ear to hear somebody over yonder who has a good voice, and when our reporters can hear in any place in the house without having to move backwards and forwards. I think it is in keeping with the dignity of parliament to hear what is going on in any part of the house.
I congratulate the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) on the new bill. I took a while to read this bill and I have been surprised by it. If hon. members have not read it there is a treat in store for them. The bill has many fine things in it. An hon. member whg spoke here last night said that we have no Canadian songs. I do not agree with him, but some of the Canadian songs do not altogether suit me because I was not bom in Canada, but I have chosen to live here. One of our great Canadians songs starts off in this way: "0 Canada, our home and native land." I looked around the other day to see if the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) was singing that and he was singing lustily. How was it his native land? Of course, there was an Irishman who said that patriotism to an Irishman is that "he is loyal to his native land whether he was bom there or not." Therefore I can sing, "O Canada, our home and native land." When our national anthem is chosen or revised they should put in a better word than "native", because it shuts out pretty nearly fifty per cent of the Canadians; but this bill is going to clear up a lot of the difficulties that exist at this time.
I have been a little anxious for some time. Sometime ago I sat on the committee of health insurance. That committee, which sat for two years, heard specialists from all over the world, from New Zealand, England, and the United States, and experts from all over Canada. I am sure the Minister of Veterans Affairs will agree with me when I say that it is the best act to be found any place, but we have not it in practice. I hope that the dominion-provincial conference will make it possible for that act to come into existence.
I now come to my own pet subject, namely, labour. Some hon. members may think it is not my pet subject, but I shall never forget when I learned to dig on the farm and when I earned my way through old Manitoba college. I started out that year wheeling brick at

fifteen cents an hour. I know what a man has to do who toils. I know the value of the money that he earns. It is not the amount of money that he earns but the use to which he puts it that counts. I should like to congratulate labour on the way they conducted themselves during the war and since V-E day. They have a right to be considered. I know we have had trouble at Windsor, but they tell me that it was not very serious trouble as compared with some of the troubles that have taken place in other places. To me there seems to be a cloud now appearing in the sky of labour. Great lakes seamen are looking for better working conditions. They may be looking for a raise in pay, but that is not their chief trouble. I would advise that ship owners and workers' representatives get together, thresh out their differences and avoid a strike.
There is one thing I do not like-and of course that does not make any difference-I do not like to see a corporation represented by a lawyer, when the future of toilers is at stake. I think it could be far better represented by a good minister, priest, clergyman or bishop who would understand the problems of the working man. I believe if that were done they would have their troubles straightened out more quickly. It would be better to have the heads of a corporation sit in on a meeting of that kind. I am convinced that if our present Minister of Labour, these corporation lawyers and the union leaders on the great lakes got together the trouble could be cleared away. This is just another case where I would hope that things could be settled before coming to a head.
I am not going to talk about labour without offering a plan, When you and I are at home we think things out. I had a group of men meet with me to formulate a plan and, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall give it to you now. This is a plan or policy for sharing the excess profits of industry and commerce with capital, labour and management. It states:
Whereas at 'this time there is grave unrest in our social structure, we are of the opinion that this matter should be studied and active steps taken to further this idea and project. We suggest that there be established by law for each industry >el>
minimum wage for labour, a. minimum salary for management and a minimum return for capital invested, and that after paying the incidental expenses of running a business or industry, and subject always to special modifications in any particular industry, the excess profits of that industry should be divided equitably among capital, labour and management in the same proportion as the minimum already specified for each of these various f actors in production.

The Address-Mr. Lalonde
We feel 'that government oversight should he exercised in each instance to make sure of the equitable character of that distribution.
We believe that more and more must the working man be taken into partnership in the industry and commerce of this country in order to secure a just return for additional effort and to give that independence of outlook which a living wage gives to every conscientious worker, -to fulfil that pledge of our war-time efforts, that the country be made a land fit for heroes to live an.
It is further stated that competition should only be allowed after capital has secured a proper return, management a proper salary, and labour ia living wage, and that all these be taken together with a fair price for goods and services as charged to the public. _ We recommend that social engineers be appointed by law to study these matters and give effect to these provisions.
I was proud to hear the Minister of Labour say on one oecasioh last year, when a strike was being discussed, that it is necessary for capital and labour to walk the same road together. That was fine. But when the three young Hebrews were cast into the fiery furnace it was found, when someone looked in, that there were four of them there-not three. One was like unto the Son of Man.
If capital and labour take the same road together they must make sure that the spirit of the Master Workman is controlling each of them, or they will not get very far. They will have a fight before they come to the end of the road.
As I said, things are in the saddle. We are living in a civilization that glorifies prosperity. Apparently we are on the threshold of the age of the bank book, when property rights, profit making, good business and prosperity are insisting that they have the right of way, leaving the traveller like the man in the parable who fell by the wayside, beaten by robbers, stripped, wounded and half dead.
I was reading a story about a great American who gave away much of his money for a special project. He said that every dollar has three kicks in it. The first kick is when you make it. As he said, "We are Yankees, and we like to make a dollar." Then he said, "The second kick is when we are sure we have it, because we have a lust for saving. The third kick is when we give it away to help somebody in need-because my mother was Irish."
So long as we allow our young men to grow with the assumption that it is with the consent of parliament, churches and municipalities that they should have power, that they should keep it who can, and that the straight road to happiness is by way of getting all the money one can, just so long jvill church and state perpetuate a policy which is sinful, unsound and superficial.
If I dared address clerics outside the house I would say to them, sweat up to your jobs; practise what you preach; live out your policy, and do not try to do it alone. Then you will be able to lead Canada into a greater life and a larger liberty.
I know what the programme is. I have great pleasure sometimes-and dear knows I make many mistakes. But I was one who, -without having to say anything about it, received extra pay at Christmas. I had a lot of fun in the Christmas season. I had more money to spend, and I spent it in a way I do not regret. I did not have any headache after and I do not expect to get the money back.
But the programme you and I must live, whether we are in this house or out of it, is: Feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, go to those in gaol; put God first, and others next. If we are not prepared to do that, then let us not listen to the prayer by Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate. However, after hearing my colleague who has just taken his seat, after hearing his words which were full of inspira-i 'in 1 felt it my duty to speak briefly in this debate. I shall confine my remarks to those of a general character, and take pleasure at the outset to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address upon their magnificent speeches.
(Translation):
I shall not needlessly take up the time of the house but I believe that I should make a few remarks in order to discuss the merits of certain proposals contained in the speech from. the throne and to offer a few suggestions to the members of the government. Therefore, my remarks will come under two separate headings. At the outset I shall say a few words on international politics and I will conclude with a few remarks of local importance.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that as the result of the last conflict, Canada has won a well-deserved place, a foremost place in the world, despite the theories of isolationists, despite the furious outcries loosed by certain nationalists of my province who were determined, at any price, to bring the ideals of my race down to the level of local and political interests. We all agree that Canada has emerged from the conflict badly shaken financially and physically. A tremendous task lies ahead; like the governments of the other countries that have suffered and that have given of
The Address-Mr. Lalonde

their best for victory, we are faced with the task of physical, spiritual and moral reconstruction.
For some years, thanks to the far-sightedness of our leader, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), we have been sending ambassadors to different countries, thus placing our country on a level with the most important nations in the world. Mr. Speaker, if the head of our government wishes to pursue this upward course towards total independence, why should we hot, as a Christian and democratic people, be represented in Rome, at the Vatican, by an official ambassador?
The speech from the throne also sets forth a policy which aims at Canada's complete freedom in the concert of nations, and the honourable the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) is sponsoring a bill by which every citizen of our country may proudly, even gloriously, claim the legitimate title of Canadian citizen. I congratulate the government on this occasion; this new gesture is but one of the numerous steps taken by the Liberal party during the past few years towards Canada's emancipation in the international sphere. Like every right-minded Canadian, I shall support this bill. It is high time that we should claim that title and that right at peace conferences and other official gatherings at which other countries are represented by envoys, delegates or ambassadors, so that our own representatives may, like those who were delegated recently, be vested with all the authority and prestige granted to the full citizens of a free state. That bill reflects credit on the government. Besides, it is consonant with the liberal tradition, and our honourable friends across the floor will have, this time at least, to be as liberal as we are.
Mr. Speaker, another matter has lately roused public opinion in my province. Some papers have expressed opinions which I re-pect; other citizens, taking advantage of their political prestige, have begun a series of meetings for the discussion of the proposed loan by our country of $1,250,000,000 to Great Britain. In my constituency, as elsewhere, as soon as that decision had been broadcast, the nationalist gang swung into action. Protests have come from the same* political ghettos where lie in hiding those who have not yet learned, after nine years of war, that the thought, in Ottawa, could not be directed along provincial channels. Some municipal council members have at once sent me resolutions protesting against that loan- of $1,250,000,000 to Great Britain, without knowing the first thing about it, without having any know-

ledge of the details or of the machinery involved. They would want me to commit myself to the point of stating, from my place in this house, that I oppose that loan. I shall do nothing of the kind, Mr. Speaker.
I shall value this legislation according to its merit in as much as it serves the interests of Canada and in the measure in which I sincerely believe that this loan is advantageous to my fellow-citizens and to the Canadian economy in general and that it may result in stabilizing the value -of the pound sterling and restoring to world economics the equilibrium which has been jeopardized by the anomalous transactions of the war.
If I am convinced that this loan may result in giving work, in my constituency, to my farmers, to my lumbermen, to all who labour for a few dollars a day; if, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this loan has been inspired by a true Canadian spirit as has been the case with the whole government policy in the last ten years, I will not hesitate to give it my earnest support.
This afternoon, I heard my colleague from Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) state that he would vote against this loan. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is taking a hasty decision. The bill has not yet been tabled; the authorized people are not yet in a position to supply all the details concerning it because the American congress is engaged in a debate on a similar matter; and we, as representatives of the Canadian people, must not ' commit ourselves officially, one way or the other. To my mind, this would prejudice our opinions before the debate in this house has been initiated.
Mr. Speaker, the economic chaos which followed the first Great War from 1929 on, was, for the most part, if we are to believe the experts of that time, attributable to the fluctuations in the value of money which resulted in an almost complete stagnation of international trade. The same economic phenomena is threatening to-day, because the English pound has fallen to the lowest level ever, because England's gold reserves have been wiped out, because Britain has been forced to recall its Canadian securities; because now, the English people, in spite of what certain nationalist groups in my province may believe, are not as wealthy as they were at the outset of the war and that Canada, due to the international stature it has grown into during the conflict, has become an indispensable cog in the proper functioning of universal economy. In a way, we have become the transmission gear of an automobile which, if it fails, causes the vehicle to stop.

In certain quarters, we are accused of trying to keep up with the Joneses, of tagging along with foreign powers in this world upheaval, and we see our Quebec nationalists, led by the Bloc Populaire-whose members are unfortunately not in the house to-night- claim that they advocate the true doctrine of nationalist charity conceived by Mr. Henri Bourassa.
Whom you defeated!

Whom we defeated. But, Mr. Speaker, the Bloc Populaire is a disgrace to real nationalist doctrine. I have no brief to defend Mr. Bourassa, but in his book entitled What Do We Owe England?, he states very plainly, on page 253 if memory serves me right, that Canada should participate in all foreign wars involving the interests of France and England, on condition that such participation be not the logical outcome of colonial bonds.
That is the nationalist doctrine advocated by our leader and by our party as well.
If we refer to the debates of 1939, we will see that we, the members of parliament of the time, declared war voluntarily without securing anyone's authorization and without being compelled to do so by colonial dependency.
What is being said in my province? People animated by unjustified1 anti-British feelings are saying exactly the opposite. One must not be afraid to say so, Mr. Speaker, although it may be against his political interests.
I mention that fact because the same propaganda is being disseminated in my province, inspired by false patriotic ideals, and through the influence of newspapers and meetings which have already been started some people want to go back to the former days of total colonialism.
I refuse to agree with them, Mr. Speaker, and will do so as long as I sit in this house. I have learned in the eleven years I have been in the Canadian House of Commons that we must examine the laws which are submitted for our approval from a federal and not a provincial point of view.
I reserve my decision in connection with that loan. After having earnestly studied the matter, I shall approve it if I find it acceptable; otherwise I shall reject it. To my mind, anyone who acts in good faith cannot commit himself in advance, on such an, important matter without going into it as fully as possible.
